scenes.narration: Rome wasn't built in a day, and it didn't fall in one either. So when did the Western Roman Empire really end?
At its largest, under the emperor Trajan, the empire covered roughly five million square kilometres. It looked permanent.

data.label: Estimated extent under Trajan, around AD 117

scenes.narration: Then came half a century of chaos. Between two hundred thirty five and two hundred eighty four, more than twenty emperors rose and fell.

data.label: More than twenty rose and fell, AD 235 to 284

scenes.narration: Power drifted east. Constantinople became a new capital in three hundred thirty. In three hundred seventy eight, Goths killed the emperor Valens at Adrianople. By three hundred ninety five, two brothers ruled two halves.

events.label: Constantinople dedicated as a new capital
Emperor Valens killed by the Goths at Adrianople
Theodosius I dies and his two sons rule East and West

scenes.narration: Then the blows came faster. Rome was sacked fifteen years after the split, and again after sixty. After eighty one years, the West was gone.
In four hundred seventy six, the general Odoacer deposed the young emperor Romulus Augustulus. He named no successor in the West.

data.caption: The date traditionally taken as the end of the Western Empire

scenes.narration: But only half of Rome fell. The western half lasted eighty one years after the split. The eastern half lasted over a thousand.

left.label: Western half
left.note: Ended in 476, when Odoacer deposed its last emperor.

right.label: Eastern half
right.note: Ended in 1453, when Constantinople fell to the Ottomans.

scenes.narration: So why did the West fall? Historians follow several threads. Constant civil war at the top. Invaders who reached Rome itself. And an empire split in two.

data.title: Threads historians follow
items: An empire divided between two courts

scenes.narration: In nineteen eighty four, the historian Alexander Demandt gathered the explanations people had offered. He counted two hundred ten.
Rome didn't fall in a day. It came apart over centuries, and half of it lasted another thousand years.

data.title: Rome didn't fall in a day
